paras: The mock trial and hanging at Anderson's Bridge took place on Saturday, about April 23, 1881, when a crowd of white men at Anderson Bridge on Lynch's Creek, near Williamsburg, South Carolina, put a Black man suspected of housebreaking through a mock trial and briefly hanged him to force a confession. He was cut down alive and later had three of the party arrested. The story, first told by the Williamsburg Herald as an affair done 'more for amusement than anything else,' ran in South Carolina papers and as a wire item in Washington and Maine.

According to the Williamsburg Herald, three young men on their way to Presbytery came upon a crowd of men at the bridge who had in their charge a 'colored man' suspected of breaking into a house and stealing from it. The man was unnamed in every account, and no officers are mentioned.

The crowd elected one of the young men, from Indiantown, as 'judge,' and 'after a fair trial' the man was convicted and sentenced 'to be swung up a little ways in order to make him confess.' A dispatch dated April 25 said the sentence was carried out: he was suspended from a tree for a few minutes and then released, 'not very much injured.' A shorter version of the dispatch added that he would not confess before he was cut down.

The man went to Scranton and took out a warrant before Trial Justice Hudson against three of the party. The dispatch reported that three of the young men were arrested, but no report of a hearing or its outcome was found.

South Carolina papers carried the Herald's paragraph without comment among state notes, the Savannah Morning News on April 25 and the Winnsboro News and Herald and Anderson Intelligencer on April 28, the latter two under or beside crime items. In that telling the proceedings were a 'fair trial' staged for amusement.

Outside the state the tone changed: the Washington National Republican headed the dispatch 'Torturing a Colored Man for Fun,' called the participants 'tormenters' and the court a 'pseudo court,' and remarked that the Presbytery-bound men 'doubtless engaged in the mock execution to vary the monotony of the trip.' The Daily Kennebec Journal in Augusta, Maine, ran a few lines under the heading 'Lynch Law,' saying the mob included 'several members of the Presbytery.'

The Herald stopped at the sentence, while the dispatch reported a hanging from a tree; the Kennebec brief also said 'members of the Presbytery' took part, where the Herald and the fuller dispatch named only young men on their way there.

reader.title: Mock trial and hanging at Anderson's Bridge
bases: A crowd seized a Black man suspected of housebreaking, staged a mock trial and suspended him from a tree for a few minutes to force a confession, then released him alive (A1, A3); no paper reports an intent to kill him.

The man was hanged briefly under a mock 'sentence' by a crowd acting without authority on a housebreaking suspicion, but he was cut down and released and was 'not very much injured' (A2, A3), so no one was killed.

The Herald item (A1, A4, A5) and the wire dispatch (A2, A3) share wording ('more for the amusement', 'swung up ... to make him confess'), so all coverage appears to trace to the Williamsburg Herald's account, though the dispatch adds details (the tree, the few minutes, the release).

accounts.label: Williamsburg Herald (reprinted in South Carolina papers)
accounts.gist: Three young men bound for Presbytery joined a crowd holding a suspected thief; 'more for amusement', one was elected judge, the man was convicted 'after a fair trial' and sentenced to be 'swung up a little ways' to make him confess; he then took out a warrant for three of the party.

accounts.label: Wire dispatch dated April 25
accounts.gist: A crowd of white men suspended the suspect from a tree for a few minutes to make him confess and then released him; he was not much injured and had three of the young men arrested.

framing.detail: The Herald text treated the affair lightly, as done 'more for amusement than anything else' and 'after a fair trial', and South Carolina papers ran it among state notes and crime items.
The National Republican's headline 'Torturing a Colored Man for Fun' and words 'tormenters', 'pseudo court' and 'mock execution' cast it as cruelty.
The Kennebec Journal ran a short wire brief headed 'Lynch Law'.
